name: Gareth Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43 and still one of the newer agents on the calls and chat queue. I finished secondary school, and I am slower than most at finding the right account page, so I use an AI helper every day to draft an answer and then check it. The queue clock bothers me more than an angry caller.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the job carrying at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Leila and I have two children in school and a mortgage. Leila works at a grocery shop, and my pay is at the lower end here. We have less than a month of expenses saved, and there are few other centres nearby, so I count each rostered hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my shift that a little AI help is useful if it keeps us from sending the wrong answer. I would also say the centre should not turn saved minutes into a faster target without asking us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job probably stays, but a quiet year does not cure our mortgage problem. I am still learning this desk and could lose hours for ordinary reasons. Leila and I do not have a full month put aside if the car breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep checking each AI draft against the account and ask a senior agent to show me one faster way to find the right page. I would put a small amount from each pay into a car-and-mortgage reserve. In the first year I would keep my shifts and stop buying lunch at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about bills even with AI doing little. One missed shift would show up at home by Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does lunch cost you over a week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is not a fortune, but it is enough to cover a school trip or the car fuel. I can pack bread and fruit without making the children feel the cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell the team you are still learning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I already ask for help when a screen makes no sense. Pretending I am quick would only leave a customer with the wrong balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team that the easy chats are the exact ones I handle best. I would join the union meeting to ask what happens to junior hours and whether training time will be paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my roster could shrink before I become good at the harder calls. The tool I use every day helps me, but it can also do the simple answers itself. With our mortgage and less than a month saved, I cannot treat a lost shift as a chance to explore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would ask to test the new answer system on paid time and record where it sends a customer back to us. I would go to the union meeting with my roster and ask for paid training on complex billing cases. In the first year, if my hours fall I would apply for a paid service job nearby, but only if the wage and hours cover our mortgage share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about the roster. I can learn fast, but the mortgage comes every month whether I pass the training or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at the union meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the junior queue should not be cut before agents get a paid chance at the hard calls. I would ask other shift workers whether their hours are already down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who could cover a missed mortgage payment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila could cover some of the food from her grocery wage, not the whole payment. We would call the lender early if hours really fell, before missing a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my shift AGI by 2028 could take our calls and chats before we finish learning another job. I would ask the union to press for written notice and paid retraining tied to actual vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior post could go first when full AGI answers customers in 2028. Robots around 2031 do not give a phone agent extra time. Leila works hard, but her grocery wage alone cannot carry our mortgage and two schoolchildren.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would attend the union meeting about notice, gather my pay slips and list local paid openings. I would ask my manager for funded training for a named vacancy, not pay for a general course from our tiny reserve. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, if my job ends I would apply for paid grocery or warehouse desk work with hours that cover our bills, and ask the lender about a temporary payment plan if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed and angry, but I can still make a list and speak to people. Less than a month saved is no landing pad for losing a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say work may change and we will keep paying for school essentials first. I would not make them carry my fear of a date on a card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only with a written offer that pays enough after housing and travel costs. I cannot move four people on the hope of a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the shift five years gives us time to ask for proper training and prove it leads to a job. I would stay in the union meetings so the newer agents have a voice when schedules change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still think my call queue could vanish with AGI in 2031. Five years might let me move into a different paid job while the children are still in school. We cannot wait for robots in 2034, because our work is mostly on the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would learn the centre’s complaint rules on paid time if my manager agrees and practise on actual cases with a senior agent. I would keep adding small amounts to the reserve and ask at union meetings for posted training routes. In the first year after 2031, if the call queue goes I would apply for a paid complaints vacancy with enough hours for our mortgage; if none exists I would search other local services while keeping any available wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but five years gives me a chance to become better at something useful. I need the route to have an actual wage at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the manager refuses paid practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current shifts and learn from the complaints I already see. I would not lose wages to study full time when the mortgage is due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children change plans because of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep their school routine steady. If our hours truly fell, Leila and I would cut extras before changing where they go to school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues a decade is enough to build a different skill if the employer pays people to learn it. I would still ask the union to watch the junior roster each year, not wait until 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 by 2036, with two children much older, but the mortgage may still be there. I could gain a real foothold in complaints work over ten years. Robots in 2039 are a later issue for other jobs; our calls face AGI first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the call shifts and ask for one paid complaint-practice session each month. I would put small sums into savings and attend union roster meetings once a year. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I would apply for a posted paid complaints role if my own calls end; I would keep working where I am until I have a written offer with enough hours and wages to cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the end of the call queue, but not trapped by the calendar. Ten years gives me a way to learn while feeding the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company will not pay for those sessions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use cases from my regular shift to learn and keep the wage. I cannot promise unpaid training time every month when we have no cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you feel more secure by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few months of mortgage payments saved and proof I can handle complex complaints. I would trust that more than a certificate with no job behind it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. A junior phone job could go before I build even one month of savings, and Leila cannot carry the mortgage alone. Paid training tied to a real vacancy, written notice and help arranging mortgage payments would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the agents who are still learning the current system. We need time with a person beside us before anyone says we failed to adapt.

headlineQuote: We need time with a person beside us before anyone says we failed to adapt.
portrait: Gareth is a **43-year-old junior** contact centre agent with secondary school education and lower pay.
He shares a mortgage and two schoolchildren with **Leila**, whose grocery wage cannot cover the home alone.
He uses AI **daily** while still learning, but has less than one month saved and few nearby centres.
He joins **union meetings** for paid training, notice and a route to actual vacancies.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his junior calls before he builds a usable reserve.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid vacancy-linked training**, written notice and help arranging mortgage payments would help.
